title: Do Fast Pit Stops Win F1 Races - or Is It Just Hype?
text:
In Formula One, every tenth of a second is sacred. Commentators often claim that pit stops decide races, but how much does a second actually matter? Does an extra moment in the pit lane truly push a driver down the finishing order, or is the fear larger than the effect?
I analysed pit-stop timing and race results across four seasons. My goal was simple. I wanted to measure the cost of one lost second.
The results were not what I expected.
Full code and reproducible scripts are available on GitHub

title: Do Fast Pit Stops Win F1 Races - or Is It Just Hype?
text:
Exploratory analysis









Most full pit cycles range from 18 to 30 seconds. Anything above 35 seconds usually signals damage, a hold at the release, a penalty or time lost behind cars entering or leaving the pits.

title: Do Fast Pit Stops Win F1 Races - or Is It Just Hype?

The regression shows that each extra second in the pit lane worsens finishing position by about 0.08 places on average. Slow stops therefore matter, but not in an explosive way. A delay of two or three seconds rarely destroys a race, but the effect compounds across a season.
Small losses are harmless alone. Repeated losses change outcomes. A quarter of a place here and half a place there becomes the difference between a podium and fourth, or between finishing in the points and missing out.
By comparison, grid position has a far stronger effect. Starting one place further back costs nearly half a finishing position. Pit time matters, but track position matters more.

Not every team pays the same price for a slow stop.
Midfield and backmarker teams such as Haas, Force India and Manor or Marussia tend to lose the most. When they fall behind, they often lack the pace to recover.
Top teams like Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes are more resilient. A slow stop hurts, but strong race pace lets them fight back. A delay becomes a setback, not a death sentence.
Slow stops do not destroy the fast. They destroy the fragile.

title: Do Fast Pit Stops Win F1 Races - or Is It Just Hype?
text:
Conclusion
Pit stops matter, but not always in the dramatic way commentary suggests. One second typically costs less than a tenth of a finishing place but the impact becomes powerful when repeated across races, seasons or drivers.
Grid position remains the strongest determinant of outcome and race pace is the engine of everything. Pit crews are not out to perform miracles, they are fighting to avoid thousands of small cuts.
In Formula One, fractions are currency, and pit time is one of them.

title: How Busy Are Melbourne’s CBD Crossings? A Statistical Deep Dive
text:
Introduction
The centre of Melbourne is full of movement and energy. Every day thousands of people pass through places like Southern Cross, Flinders Street, and QV Melbourne. At first glance it feels chaotic. Underneath that movement however is a pattern. I wanted to understand those patterns and tell a story about how these three locations behave.
I approached this like a real analytics problem. Start with descriptive exploration. Fit distributions that reflect the character of each location. Estimate meaningful quantities for planning and design. Compare sites in a way that answers the practical questions that planners and marketers actually care about. By the end of the analysis, these three crossings no longer felt like random busy spots on a map. They felt like distinct personalities with their own rhythms and their own commercial and operational implications.

title: How Busy Are Melbourne’s CBD Crossings? A Statistical Deep Dive
text:
Final Thoughts
What started as a simple exploration turned into a deeper look at how Melbourne moves. Each crossing behaves differently and those differences matter. They influence engineering decisions, marketing opportunities, and even the reliability of revenue estimates.
Southern Cross is steady. Flinders Street is slightly lower but similar in structure. QV Melbourne is on its own path with heavy traffic and large fluctuations that give it both challenges and commercial potential. Data lets us see these places as more than busy intersections. They become systems with measurable behaviour and predictable characteristics. That is what makes this type of analysis rewarding. It connects statistical modelling to real city life.

title: Who Actually Turns Up? Measuring Member Engagement from Event Registrations
text:
For my industry placement in the Monash University Master of Business Analytics, I worked with a South Australian peak body for professional educator associations. The organisation could already say which member associations took part in its events. It could not say who attended, how often, or how that compared with last year.
I built a person-level engagement model and an interactive dashboard from the organisation’s event registration records. Staff can now pick any year and see engagement for individuals, associations and sector cohorts, and the association results agree closely with the records they had been keeping by hand.

title: Who Actually Turns Up? Measuring Member Engagement from Event Registrations
text:
For my industry placement in the Monash University Master of Business Analytics, I worked with a South Australian peak body for professional educator associations. The organisation could already say which member associations took part in its events. It could not say who attended, how often, or how that compared with last year.
I built a person-level engagement model and an interactive dashboard from the organisation’s event registration records. Staff can now pick any year and see engagement for individuals, associations and sector cohorts, and the association results agree closely with the records they had been keeping by hand.

title: Who Actually Turns Up? Measuring Member Engagement from Event Registrations
text:
The problem
Engagement was tracked by hand in a yearly spreadsheet: one tick per association per event. A tick showed that an association took part. It did not show who came or how many times, and one year’s sheet could not be compared with another’s.

title: Who Actually Turns Up? Measuring Member Engagement from Event Registrations
text:
My approach


  
    1 · Raw exports
    34,037
    rows in 8 files
  
  
    2 · Clean
    11,890
    registrations, 184 events
  
  
    3 · Match people
    4,249
    identities, down from 6,282
  
  
    4 · Score + dashboard
    4 tiers
    5-tab Shiny app
  

From raw ticketing exports to a dashboard staff can use.

Getting to one clean dataset. The raw material was eight overlapping exports from the Humanitix ticketing platform (34,037 rows and 504 columns), plus a membership register and staff review spreadsheets. I deduplicated the exports to 25,217 tickets, kept only member-engagement events, and coalesced about 95 inconsistently named registration-form columns into five clean fields. The final dataset holds 11,890 registrations by 4,211 people across 184 events, from March 2021 to August 2026.
Working out who is who. This was the hardest part. There was no reliable unique ID, and email addresses were often shared office accounts. I built a person key from standardised names plus organisation. To merge spelling variants of the same organisation I used Jaro-Winkler fuzzy matching with hierarchical clustering, then added a step that assigns each person their best known organisation. That step alone cut the identity count from 6,282 to 4,249. Staff then reviewed the edge cases.
Keeping the model simple. My first version was a weighted score combining recency, frequency and tenure. After discussing it with the client, I replaced it with something anyone can explain: the number of events a person attended, in four tiers.



Events attended
Tier
What it means




1
Dormant
Came once


2
At risk
Came back, but not often


3 to 5
Engaged
A regular


6 or more
Highly engaged

I extended the same idea to associations, using a coverage rate (the share of events with at least one attendee from that association), and to 12 sector cohorts.

title: Who Actually Turns Up? Measuring Member Engagement from Event Registrations
text:
The result
A model the organisation can trust. Association coverage from my model agreed with the organisation’s own hand-kept records, with rank correlations of 0.91 to 0.92 in each full year.
A dashboard staff can use. The five-tab R Shiny app recalculates every measure for any year: an overview, association engagement, cohorts, an individual explorer, and a list of committee members who have never attended an event.
A pipeline that can be rerun. The whole pipeline is written in Quarto. The report renders from small aggregate tables, so it needs no personal data. Along the way I found and fixed a locale-dependent bug that changed row counts between runs.

title: Who Actually Turns Up? Measuring Member Engagement from Event Registrations
text:
What I learned

Identity comes before analysis. Every number downstream depended on deciding who counted as one person, so that is where most of the careful work went.
The simpler model was the better one. The weighted score was harder to explain than a count of events, and the client chose the one they could explain.
Check against what people already know. Agreement with the hand-kept records is what made the new numbers credible.
Reproducible means the same answer every time. A row count that shifted between runs was a bug worth chasing down.

Tools: R, tidyverse, stringdist, Shiny, bslib, plotly, DT, Quarto, Git.

title: Did Closing Police Station Counters Increase Crime in Victoria?
text:
In late 2023, Victoria Police reduced public reception counter hours at 43 stations across the state, framing the move as a way to free up officers for street patrols. The policy rolled out in two main phases: 23 stations from November 2023, and a further 20 from January 2024.
The stated logic was simple: fewer officers staffing front counters means more officers on the street, which should deter crime. But does the data support that?
This is a live policy debate. In June 2026, the Herald Sun reported that crime had risen 22.4% in areas with reduced station hours, faster than in the rest of the state, and Victoria Police rejected any link between counter hours and crime. A further round of cuts in Melbourne’s outer north had taken effect only days earlier. I wanted to test the claim properly using a causal inference framework rather than a simple before-and-after comparison.

title: Did Closing Police Station Counters Increase Crime in Victoria?
text:
In late 2023, Victoria Police reduced public reception counter hours at 43 stations across the state, framing the move as a way to free up officers for street patrols. The policy rolled out in two main phases: 23 stations from November 2023, and a further 20 from January 2024.
The stated logic was simple: fewer officers staffing front counters means more officers on the street, which should deter crime. But does the data support that?
This is a live policy debate. In June 2026, the Herald Sun reported that crime had risen 22.4% in areas with reduced station hours, faster than in the rest of the state, and Victoria Police rejected any link between counter hours and crime. A further round of cuts in Melbourne’s outer north had taken effect only days earlier. I wanted to test the claim properly using a causal inference framework rather than a simple before-and-after comparison.

title: Did Closing Police Station Counters Increase Crime in Victoria?
text:
Data
All crime data comes from the Crime Statistics Agency Victoria, an independent body that publishes recorded criminal incidents by local government area (LGA) annually (year ending March). The dataset covers all 79 Victorian LGAs from 2017 to 2026.
The station closure list was compiled from Victoria Police’s own November 2023 public announcement, which named all 43 affected stations and their revised hours. The May 2026 cuts fall after the end of the data and are not part of the analysis. Each station was mapped to its LGA to build a treatment group of 34 LGAs.

title: Did Closing Police Station Counters Increase Crime in Victoria?
text:
Method
I used a difference-in-differences (DiD) design, which compares the change in crime in treated LGAs (those with reduced hours) against the change in control LGAs (those that kept full hours), over the same period. This controls for statewide trends such as cost-of-living pressures and post-COVID crime recovery, which would have affected all LGAs regardless of the policy.
The model includes LGA fixed effects (controlling for permanent differences between areas) and year fixed effects (controlling for statewide shocks), with standard errors clustered by LGA.
The outcome is the log of recorded incidents, so the estimate reads as a percentage change. This matters because treated LGAs are much larger than control LGAs, averaging roughly 7,800 incidents a year against 3,000. A model in raw counts would mistake that difference in size for a difference in trend.



DiD estimate: change in recorded criminal incidents in treated LGAs, with 95 percent interval

title: Did Closing Police Station Counters Increase Crime in Victoria?
text:
Checking the Key Assumption
The critical assumption in DiD is parallel trends: that treated and control LGAs were following the same crime trajectory before the policy. To check it, I estimated the gap between the two groups separately for every year, relative to 2023, the last year before the reductions. If the assumption holds, the gaps before 2023 should sit close to zero.









The assumption holds only loosely. No single pre-policy year is significantly different from zero at the 5% level, but the gap drifts downward, from about 9% above the 2023 gap in 2017 to about 6% below it in 2022, and the six pre-policy years are jointly significant (p = 0.007). Treated LGAs were not on exactly the same path as the controls.
What the plot does show clearly is the timing. The gap is flat in 2024, which covers only the first two to four months of reduced hours, then jumps to around 11% in 2025 and 2026, larger than any pre-policy movement.

title: Did Closing Police Station Counters Increase Crime in Victoria?
text:
Results
After accounting for LGA and year fixed effects, treated LGAs recorded approximately 5% more criminal incidents than would have been expected had they followed the control group trend (95% interval 0.1% to 10.2%, p = 0.047). The result is significant at the 5% level, but only just, and the imperfect pre-policy trends mean it should be read as suggestive rather than conclusive.
The direction is consistent with the Herald Sun’s finding, though the size of the effect is much smaller than a raw before-and-after comparison implies.

Which offences moved?
If shorter counter hours matter, the effect should not be spread evenly across every kind of crime. I ran the same model separately for five common offence types, this time on recorded offences rather than incidents.

Theft, assault, robbery and disorderly conduct are all statistically indistinguishable from zero, with wide intervals. The overall increase therefore looks concentrated in property crime rather than violence or public order.

title: Did Closing Police Station Counters Increase Crime in Victoria?
text:
Limitations

Recorded crime is not the same as crime. A closed counter could change how much crime gets reported as well as how much occurs. If anything, fewer walk-in reports would push recorded crime down, which would make these estimates conservative, but the data cannot separate the two.
Stations were not chosen at random. Victoria Police selected which counters to cut, and the pre-policy trends were not perfectly parallel. Something else that differs between the two groups after 2023 could explain part of the gap.
LGAs are a coarse unit. A treated LGA can contain several stations that kept full hours, so the analysis measures the effect of having at least one reduced counter, not of living near one.
The post-policy window is short. There are three data years after the change, and the first covers only a few months of reduced hours.

title: Did Closing Police Station Counters Increase Crime in Victoria?
text:
Conclusion
Areas where Victoria Police cut reception hours recorded around 5% more criminal incidents afterwards than comparable areas, with the increase appearing from 2025 and concentrated in burglary. That is in the direction critics of the policy have claimed, but it is much smaller than the headline figures, only just statistically significant, and rests on an assumption the data supports imperfectly. The evidence is enough to question the claim that the changes had no effect on community safety, and not enough to say with confidence that they caused crime to rise.
